questions.q: A line makes errors $y_i - \hat{y}_i = 1, -2, 3$ on three points. What is the **MSE** $L = \frac{1}{n}\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$?
questions.explain: Square each error ($1, 4, 9$), sum to $14$, divide by $n = 3$: $14/3 \approx 4.67$. $2$ is the MAE (mean of $|e_i|$), $0.67$ forgets to square/abs (signs cancel: $2/3$), and $14$ forgets to divide by $n$.

questions.q: In the lab you drag a single point far away from the line. Which statement best describes what happens?
options: MAE jumps more than MSE, because absolute values are larger than squares
MSE jumps much more than MAE, because the outlier's error is squared
Both losses grow by exactly the same amount
Neither loss changes, since only one point moved
questions.explain: MSE squares errors: being off by 10 costs 100 while being off by 2 costs only 4, so one outlier can explode it. MAE grows only linearly with the distance, which is why it is called robust to outliers.

questions.q: Why is MAE described as harder to use with calculus than MSE?
options: Its V-shaped absolute value has a sharp, non-smooth tip at zero error
It can be negative, so minimizing it never stops
It has no minimum at all
It needs the errors to be squared first
questions.explain: $|e|$ has a kink at $e = 0$ where the derivative jumps from $-1$ to $+1$. MSE is smooth everywhere ($e^2 \to 2e$). MAE is still non-negative and does have a minimum.

questions.q: What does a loss function hand back to the training process?
options: A list containing the corrected predictions
The best possible slope $w$ and bias $b$ directly
The probability that the model is correct
A single number summarizing how bad all the predictions are — lower is better
questions.explain: The loss 'crushes' all the individual mistakes into one score. Training then searches for the parameters ($w$, $b$) that make this score as small as possible; the loss itself does not give those parameters.
